Let $A$ be a complex vector space with a complex-bilinear associative product, unit $1_A$, and conjugate-linear involution satisfying $(ab)^*=b^*a^*$, $(a^*)^*=a$ and $1_A^*=1_A$. Let $\omega:A\to\mathbb C$ be complex-linear with $\omega(1_A)=1$ and real nonnegative $\omega(a^*a)$ for every $a\in A$. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function. Put $N_\omega:=\{a\in A:\omega(a^*a)=0\}$ and $\mathcal D_\omega:=A/N_\omega$, with

$$([a],[b])_\omega:=\omega(b^*a),$$

using the first-variable-linear convention. Let $H_\omega$ be the Hilbert completion of this inner-product space, and identify $\mathcal D_\omega$ with its canonical dense image in $H_\omega$. For each $a\in A$ define left multiplication on the common domain $\mathcal D_\omega$ by $\pi_\omega(a)[b]:=[ab]$. Then $\pi_\omega$ is a unital algebra representation of $A$ on the invariant dense domain $\mathcal D_\omega$, and

$$\mathcal D_\omega\subseteq D(\pi_\omega(a)^*),\qquad \pi_\omega(a)^*|_{\mathcal D_\omega}=\pi_\omega(a^*).$$

Each $\pi_\omega(a)$ is closable, meaning that the closure of its graph in $H_\omega\times H_\omega$ is the graph of an operator. The vector $\Omega_\omega:=[1_A]$ is a unit cyclic vector, $\pi_\omega(A)\Omega_\omega=\mathcal D_\omega$, and $\omega(a)=(\pi_\omega(a)\Omega_\omega,\Omega_\omega)$. For uniqueness, let $K$ be a Hilbert space, $\mathcal D'\subseteq K$ a dense linear subspace invariant under every operator $\rho(a)$, and $\rho:A\to\operatorname{End}(\mathcal D')$ a unital algebra representation satisfying $(\rho(a)x,y)=(x,\rho(a^*)y)$ for all $a\in A$ and $x,y\in\mathcal D'$. If $\Omega'\in\mathcal D'$, $\mathcal D'=\rho(A)\Omega'$, and $\omega(a)=(\rho(a)\Omega',\Omega')$, then there is a unique unitary $V:H_\omega\to K$ with $V\Omega_\omega=\Omega'$ and $V\pi_\omega(a)x=\rho(a)Vx$ for all $a\in A$ and $x\in\mathcal D_\omega$. This theorem supplies neither a C*-norm nor essential self-adjointness of $\pi_\omega(a)$ when $a=a^*$.
steps: By [F1], $N_\omega$ is a subspace and every element of it pairs to zero with every element of $A$. Thus $([a],[b])_\omega=\omega(b^*a)$ is independent of both representatives; it is Hermitian and nonnegative, and $([a],[a])_\omega=0$ holds exactly when $a\in N_\omega$, so the quotient pairing is positive definite. [F1, given]

For $a,b\in A$, replacing $b$ by $b+n$ with $n\in N_\omega$ changes $ab$ by $an\in N_\omega$ because $N_\omega$ is a left ideal by [F1]; hence $\pi_\omega(a)[b]=[ab]$ is well defined. Bilinearity, associativity and $1_A$ give $\pi_\omega(a+b)=\pi_\omega(a)+\pi_\omega(b)$, $\pi_\omega(\lambda a)=\lambda\pi_\omega(a)$, $\pi_\omega(ab)=\pi_\omega(a)\pi_\omega(b)$ and $\pi_\omega(1_A)=I_{\mathcal D_\omega}$, and left multiplication keeps $\mathcal D_\omega$ invariant. [F1, given, algebra]

Apply [F2] to the quotient inner-product space $\mathcal D_\omega$; under the stated Countable Choice assumption this gives the Hilbert completion $H_\omega$ and a dense isometric embedding of $\mathcal D_\omega$, which we identify with its image. This is the only completion invoked. [F2, given, step 1.1]

For $a,b,c\in A$, the quotient form gives $(\pi_\omega(a)[b],[c])_\omega=\omega(c^*ab)=([b],\pi_\omega(a^*)[c])_\omega$. By the definition of the Hilbert-space adjoint, this identity for all $[b]\in\mathcal D_\omega$ shows $[c]\in D(\pi_\omega(a)^*)$ and $\pi_\omega(a)^*[c]=\pi_\omega(a^*)[c]$. [step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

Since $([1_A],[1_A])_\omega=\omega(1_A)=1$, $\Omega_\omega$ is a unit vector. Also $\pi_\omega(a)\Omega_\omega=[a]$ for every $a\in A$, so its algebraic orbit is exactly $\mathcal D_\omega$ and is dense. Finally $(\pi_\omega(a)\Omega_\omega,\Omega_\omega)_\omega=([a],[1_A])_\omega=\omega(a)$, recovering the state. [given, step 1.1, step 1.2]

Let $(H',\mathcal D',\rho,\Omega')$ be another algebraically cyclic *-representation of $A$ with common invariant dense domain $\mathcal D'=\rho(A)\Omega'$, $\rho(a^*)=\rho(a)^*|_{\mathcal D'}$, and $\omega(a)=(\rho(a)\Omega',\Omega')$. Define $U[a]:=\rho(a)\Omega'$. If $[a]=[0]$, then $\|\rho(a)\Omega'\|^2=\omega(a^*a)=0$, so $U$ is well defined; and for $a,b\in A$, $(U[a],U[b])=\omega(b^*a)=([a],[b])_\omega$ by the representation's adjoint identity. Thus $U$ is an isometry from $\mathcal D_\omega$ onto the dense subspace $\mathcal D'$. [given, F1, step 1.1, step 1.2]

Suppose $x_n\in\mathcal D_\omega$, $x_n\to0$ in $H_\omega$, and $\pi_\omega(a)x_n\to y$ in $H_\omega$. For each $z\in\mathcal D_\omega$, step 2.2 gives $(y,z)_\omega=\lim_n(\pi_\omega(a)x_n,z)_\omega=\lim_n(x_n,\pi_\omega(a^*)z)_\omega=0$. Density forces $y=0$. Therefore the closed graph relation of $\pi_\omega(a)$ contains no two distinct outputs over one input: their difference would be a nonzero pair $(0,y)$. The graph closure is a graph, so $\pi_\omega(a)$ is closable. In particular, if $a=a^*$ then $\pi_\omega(a)$ is symmetric on $\mathcal D_\omega$; this does not prove essential self-adjointness. [step 2.2, given]

The isometry extends uniquely from the dense domain to a unitary $\overline U:H_\omega\to H'$ because its range $\mathcal D'$ is dense. It sends $\Omega_\omega$ to $\Omega'$ and, for $[b]\in\mathcal D_\omega$, $\overline U\pi_\omega(a)[b]=\rho(ab)\Omega'=\rho(a)\overline U[b]$; hence it intertwines the representations on the common domains. Uniqueness follows because every vector of $\mathcal D_\omega$ has the form $\pi_\omega(a)\Omega_\omega$. [step 2.3, step 2.4, step 1.2] ∎

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ of [[def-countable-choice]]. On $M=\mathbb R^4$ with global coordinates $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, set $\eta_{ab}=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, orient $M$ by $o=dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and use $\partial_0$ to select the standard future cone. Coordinates have length units, derivatives have inverse-length units, and the Fourier phase and conformal factor are dimensionless, consistent with [[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. Thus $\Box_\eta$, $\Box_g$, $R_g$, and $P_g$ have inverse-length-squared units. Let $\Omega\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^4;(0,\infty))$ be real and dimensionless, and define the prescribed external Lorentzian metric $g_{ab}=\Omega^2\eta_{ab}$. No field equation for $g$ is assumed. Write $d\mathrm{vol}_g=\Omega^4d^4x$ for its positive integration density and $\Box_\eta=\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b$. Let $R_g$ be the scalar curvature with the convention of [[def-gr-curvature-tensor-and-derived-tensors]], which is also used by [[thm-emg-conformal-einstein-transformation]], and define
$$\Box_g h:=\Omega^{-4}\partial_a\!\left(\Omega^2\eta^{ab}\partial_bh\right),\qquad P_g:=\Box_g-\frac16R_g.$$
The test space is $\mathcal D=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C)$ with the LF test-function topology of [[def-test-function-topology]]. Let $\Phi_0$ be the massless Minkowski Fock field and let $\varpi_0\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ be its normalized vacuum vector, written $|0\rangle$ in Dirac notation. The common dense invariant domain and field convention are those of [[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]] and [[lem-qft-scalar-causal-commutator]]. For $f\in\mathcal D$, define the curved-background smeared field by
$$\Phi_g(f):=\Phi_0(\Omega^3f).$$

Then, with all equalities understood on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ or as distributional equalities as appropriate:

1. The exact curvature and scalar wave identities are
$$R_g=-6\Omega^{-3}\Box_\eta\Omega,\qquad P_g(\Omega^{-1}u)=\Omega^{-3}\Box_\eta u\quad(u\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^4;\mathbb C)).$$

2. The map $f\mapsto\Phi_g(f)$ is a weak operator-valued distribution on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, meaning that for every $\chi,\psi\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ the map $f\mapsto\langle\chi,\Phi_g(f)\psi\rangle_2$ is a continuous complex-linear functional on $\mathcal D$ with its test-function topology. It satisfies $\Phi_g(P_gf)=0$ for every $f\in\mathcal D$. The normalized Minkowski vacuum defines a positive state on the finite polynomial $*$-algebra generated by the real-test fields.

3. If $\operatorname{supp}f$ and $\operatorname{supp}h$ are spacelike separated (every pair of points in the two supports has positive $\eta$-squared separation), then $[\Phi_g(f),\Phi_g(h)]=0$ on $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$.

4. The two-point distribution relative to $d\mathrm{vol}_g(x)d\mathrm{vol}_g(y)$ is
$$W_g(x,y)=\Omega(x)^{-1}\Omega(y)^{-1}W_0(x,y),$$
where $W_0$ is the massless Minkowski Fock-vacuum two-point distribution from [[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]], relative to $d^4x\,d^4y$ and paired bilinearly as $W_0(f,h)=\langle\varpi_0,\Phi_0(f)\Phi_0(h)\varpi_0\rangle_2$. On compact tests, $P_g$ is formally symmetric for $d\mathrm{vol}_g$.

This is a selected free-field representation obtained from one Minkowski Fock vacuum. It asserts no uniqueness of a curved-spacetime state, generic Hadamard-state existence, thermal-state result, renormalized stress-tensor transformation, massive or minimally coupled result, Einstein equation, or backreaction claim. The metric is prescribed background data, not a dynamical solution.
steps: Put $u_a=\Omega^{-1}\partial_a\Omega$. Since $\eta_{ab}$ is constant, [F14] gives $\Gamma^a{}_{bc}(\eta)=0$. Coordinate fields commute, so the curvature definition [F2] gives $R(\partial_c,\partial_d)\partial_b=0$ for all indices; every curvature component and its Ricci and scalar contractions therefore vanish, in particular $S_\eta=0$. Thus for the base metric $\eta$, $\nabla=\partial$, $\theta=\eta^{ab}\partial_a u_b$, and $s=\eta^{ab}u_au_b$ in [F3]. Applying that conformal formula gives $R_g=-6\Omega^{-2}(\eta^{ab}\partial_a u_b+\eta^{ab}u_au_b)$. Since $\partial_a u_b=\Omega^{-1}\partial_a\partial_b\Omega-\Omega^{-2}(\partial_a\Omega)(\partial_b\Omega)$ and $u_au_b=\Omega^{-2}(\partial_a\Omega)(\partial_b\Omega)$, the gradient-square terms cancel, giving $R_g=-6\Omega^{-3}\Box_\eta\Omega$. Thus $f\mapsto\Omega^3f$ is continuous $\mathcal D_K\to\mathcal S$ by [F11,F12]. Each generator preserves $\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$, so finite products and linear combinations do too; repeated use of symmetry gives $\langle\chi,B\psi\rangle_2=\langle B^*\chi,\psi\rangle_2$ for every polynomial $B$ and $\chi,\psi\in\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$. Define $\omega_g(B):=\langle\varpi_0,B\varpi_0\rangle_2$. Then $\omega_g(B^*B)=\langle B\varpi_0,B\varpi_0\rangle_2=\|B\varpi_0\|^2\ge0$, and $\omega_g(1)=1$. [given, A2, F1, F4, construct]

At every point $g(v,v)=\Omega^2\eta(v,v)$, so the future causal cones for $g$ and $\eta$ coincide and use the direction selected by $\partial_0$. Define causal reachability by piecewise $C^1$ curves whose tangent is future-causal on each smooth piece, allowing constant curves; such a curve is admissible for $g$ exactly when it is admissible for $\eta$. In $(-+++)$ coordinates a future causal tangent satisfies $\dot x^0\ge|\dot{\mathbf x}|$; integrating along each piece and using the triangle inequality gives $|\Delta\mathbf x|\le\Delta x^0$ for a future causal curve. Conversely, if $\Delta x^0\ge|\Delta\mathbf x|$, the straight segment has future causal tangent (including the constant segment when the endpoints agree). Reversing endpoints handles the past direction. Thus two points are causally related exactly when their coordinate difference has nonpositive $\eta$-squared norm, for both $g$ and $\eta$; positive-$\eta$-squared pairs are spacelike for both. [given, A1, algebra]

Thus $\Box_gh=\Omega^{-4}\partial_a(\Omega^2\partial^ah)$, where $\partial^a=\eta^{ab}\partial_b$. Write $f=f_R+if_I$ and $h=h_R+ih_I$ with real compact tests. Their supports and the supports of $\Omega^3f_R,\Omega^3f_I,\Omega^3h_R,\Omega^3h_I$ lie in the original spacelike-separated support sets by step 1.2; step 1.4 confirms that these pairs are spacelike for $g$ as well as $\eta$. constructed two-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^2$ with
inner product
$\langle x,y\rangle=x_0\overline{y_0}+x_1\overline{y_1}$, linear in the
first variable. Let $e_0=(1,0)$, $e_1=(0,1)$ and
$v=\alpha e_0+\beta e_1$ with
$|\alpha|^2+|\beta|^2=1$. Prepare the rank-one density operator
$\rho=T_{v,v}$, where
$T_{v,v}x=\langle x,v\rangle v$ as in
[[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]]. Define the two measurement
operators

$$P_0=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad M_{0,1}=P_0,\quad M_{1,1}=P_1.$$

This is a finite normalized instrument. The postulate
[[post-qft-constructed-model-and-measurement]] assigns model probabilities
$p_0=|\alpha|^2$ and $p_1=|\beta|^2$, which sum to one. When $p_i>0$ its
conditional state is $P_i$; when $p_i=0$ the normalized update is undefined.
This is a conditional model calculation, not a report of an observed result.

For the formal comparison, let $g$ be an indeterminate; the formal algebra
assigns it no SI unit or numerical value. The formal series

$$F(g):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}n!g^n\in\mathbb R\llbracket g\rrbracket$$

has a coefficient for every $n$, while its numerical power series has radius
zero after the real coefficients are embedded in $\mathbb C$ for evaluation.
This example separates coefficient data from numerical convergence.
The Born postulate does not assign an exact probability to a coefficient in
isolation: an additional map from formal data to a constructed state and
measurement, together with any approximation and error assumptions, would be
needed. No such map or observed outcome is claimed.

Assume the Countable Choice axiom $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $d\ge1$, $T>0$, $\hbar>0$, and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$. Let $H_0=H_0^\dagger$ be a $d\times d$ Hermitian matrix with entries in joules, and let $V:[0,T]\to M_d(\mathbb C)$ be norm-continuous, Hermitian-valued, and in joules. Define
$$V_I(t)=e^{itH_0/\hbar}V(t)e^{-itH_0/\hbar},\qquad B=\sup_{0\le t\le T}\|V_I(t)\|,\qquad z=\frac{|\lambda|BT}{\hbar}.$$
The coupling $\lambda$ is dimensionless and $z$ is dimensionless. Put $S_0(t)=I$ and
$$S_{n+1}(t)=-\frac{i}{\hbar}\int_0^t V_I(r)S_n(r)\,dr,\qquad S(t)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\lambda^nS_n(t).$$
Then the series converges in operator norm on $[0,T]$, $S$ is the unique solution of $\dot S=-i\lambda V_I S/\hbar$, $S(0)=I$, and $S(t)$ is unitary. For every $N\ge0$,
$$\left\|S(T)-\sum_{n=0}^N\lambda^nS_n(T)\right\| \le e^z\frac{z^{N+1}}{(N+1)!}.$$

Define $S(T;\lambda)=I+iT(\lambda)$ and $T(\lambda)=\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda^nT_n$. For every pair of basis indices $f,i$, exact unitarity gives
$$2\,\operatorname{Im}T_{ii}(\lambda)=\sum_f|T_{fi}(\lambda)|^2,$$
and coefficient comparison gives $T_1=T_1^\dagger$ and $2\,\operatorname{Im}T_2=T_1^\dagger T_1$. These are identities for this finite matrix model.

For $H=g_E\sigma_x$ on $\mathbb C^2$, where $g_E>0$ is in joules and $\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, the evolution matrix is
$$e^{-itH/\hbar}=\cos(g_Et/\hbar)I-i\sin(g_Et/\hbar)\sigma_x.$$
Its exact off-diagonal matrix-element square is $\sin^2(g_Et/\hbar)$; its first-order squared coefficient is $(g_Et/\hbar)^2$, which can exceed $1$. For every positive rate $\Gamma$ in $\mathrm{s}^{-1}$, the survival matrix-element square $\cos^2(g_Et/\hbar)$ is not $e^{-\Gamma t}$.

For an integer $N\ge0$, on the finite basis $|0\rangle,\ldots,|N\rangle$ define $a_N|n\rangle=\sqrt n\,|n-1\rangle$ (zero at $n=0$) and $a_N^\dagger|n\rangle=\sqrt{n+1}|n+1\rangle$ for $n<N$, with $a_N^\dagger|N\rangle=0$. Then
$$[a_N,a_N^\dagger]=I-(N+1)|N\rangle\langle N|.$$
No finite-dimensional matrices can satisfy $[A,B]=I$, because the trace of a commutator is zero while the trace of $I$ is the dimension.
steps: The matrix exponential is defined by its norm-convergent power series; termwise differentiation on compact time intervals gives $W'(t)=iH_0W(t)/\hbar$ for $W(t)=e^{itH_0/\hbar}$. Hence $(W(t)^\dagger W(t))'=0$ and $W(0)^\dagger W(0)=I$, so $W$ is unitary (in finite dimension a left inverse is an inverse). Therefore $V_I(t)=W(t)V(t)W(t)^\dagger$ is Hermitian and norm-continuous. Its norm is bounded on compact $[0,T]$, so $B<\infty$. [given, F1, algebra]

Recursion expresses $\lambda^nS_n(T)$ as an $n$-fold ordered integral with integrand of norm at most $(|\lambda|B/\hbar)^n$. The volume of $0<t_n<\cdots<t_1<T$ is $T^n/n!$: induction integrates the preceding volume $t^{n-1}/(n-1)!$ from $0$ to $T$. Thus $\|\lambda^nS_n(T)\|\le z^n/n!$ and the same bound with $T$ replaced by any $t\in[0,T]$ holds uniformly. The scalar exponential series proves uniform absolute convergence. [given, F1, algebra]

For $\sigma_x^2=I$, separate the even and odd powers in the absolutely convergent exponential series: $$e^{-iz\sigma_x}=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-1)^kz^{2k}}{(2k)!}I -i\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-1)^kz^{2k+1}}{(2k+1)!}\sigma_x =\cos z\,I-i\sin z\,\sigma_x,$$ where $z=g_Et/\hbar$. Its off-diagonal entry has modulus square $\sin^2z$, and the first-order term has modulus square $z^2$. Taking $|z|>1$ makes the latter exceed $1$. Also $\cos^2z$ has derivative $0$ at $t=0$, whereas $e^{-\Gamma t}$ has derivative $-\Gamma<0$ there; so they cannot agree for all $t$ when $\Gamma>0$. [given, F1, algebra]

For the tail, write $n=N+1+k$. Then $$\sum_{n=N+1}^\infty\frac{z^n}{n!} =\frac{z^{N+1}}{(N+1)!}\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{z^k}{(N+2)\cdots(N+1+k)} \le \frac{z^{N+1}}{(N+1)!}\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{z^k}{k!} =e^z\frac{z^{N+1}}{(N+1)!},$$ where an empty product is $1$ and $(N+2)\cdots(N+1+k)\ge k!$. The norm tail is bounded by this scalar tail. [step 1.2, algebra]

The family $\mathcal H(t)=\lambda V_I(t)$ satisfies the exact hypotheses of [F2] and [F3] on the compact interval $[0,T]$: it is bounded, norm-continuous and self-adjoint, and the required $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is [A1]. The recursion above is its Dyson recursion, so [F2] supplies the Volterra equation and uniqueness, [F3] supplies unitarity of $S(t)$, and step 1.2 supplies the displayed sharper bound with $B$. [given, A1, F2, F3, step 1.2]

From $S=I+iT$, $S^\dagger S=I$ expands to $i(T-T^\dagger)+T^\dagger T=0$. Its $ii$ entry is $-2\,\operatorname{Im}T_{ii}+\sum_f|T_{fi}|^2=0$, proving the exact identity. The norm-convergent power series makes $T(\lambda)$ analytic near $0$ (indeed entire), so coefficient comparison is valid: the $\lambda$ term gives $T_1=T_1^\dagger$, and the $\lambda^2$ term gives $i(T_2-T_2^\dagger)+T_1^\dagger T_1=0$, hence $2\,\operatorname{Im}T_2=T_1^\dagger T_1$. [step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra]

For the linear truncation $S_{\rm tr}=I+i\lambda T_1$ with $T_1=T_1^\dagger$, multiplication gives $S_{\rm tr}^\dagger S_{\rm tr}=I+\lambda^2T_1^2$. If $\lambda T_1\ne0$, then $T_1^2$ is nonzero positive semidefinite because $\langle T_1^2v,v\rangle=\|T_1v\|^2$; hence this truncation is not unitary. The exact coefficient relation in step 3.1 therefore requires the higher-order correction whenever its right side is nonzero. [step 3.1, algebra]

For $n<N$, direct application gives $a_Na_N^\dagger|n\rangle=(n+1)|n\rangle$ and $a_N^\dagger a_N|n\rangle=n|n\rangle$, so the commutator equals $|n\rangle$. At $n=N$, the two terms are $0$ and $N|N\rangle$, so their difference is $-N|N\rangle$. These are exactly the values of $I-(N+1)|N\rangle\langle N|$ on each basis vector. Use the framework-local unit and domain dictionary of
[[def-qft-framework-units]] and the energy, SI/natural-unit, and finite-matrix
conventions of [[def-qft-example-data]]. A physical quantity is always typed
relative to the selected QFT formulation and its declared model data; its name
or units alone do not identify it with a quantity in another formulation.

For the **exact finite-regulator class** used on this page, the state space is
the finite-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathcal H=\mathbb C^d$ for an integer
$d\ge1$. Model inputs include the selected Hermitian Hamiltonian matrices,
their time-dependent Hermitian interaction when present, a dimensionless
coupling parameter, an initial state, and an explicitly supplied finite
outcome measurement. A pure initial state is a vector $\psi\in\mathbb C^d$
with $\|\psi\|=1$; a mixed state is a matrix $\rho=\rho^*$ with
$\langle\rho v,v\rangle\ge0$ for every $v$ and $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$.
An exact regulated observable on this finite space is a specified Hermitian
matrix $O=O^*$ with a declared physical unit. The matrix and state are model
data; the measurement procedure and any physical rule assigning outcomes are
additional data. This definition does not say that an operator symbol by
itself is a detector outcome or probability.

A **finite probability law** on the declared outcome set
$\{1,\ldots,m\}$, $m\ge1$, is a vector $(p_1,\ldots,p_m)$ with
$p_a\ge0$ and $\sum_{a=1}^m p_a=1$. It is a mathematical type. Assigning that
law to a particular preparation and measurement is a separate physical
postulate. A prediction derived from an actually constructed regulated model
is conditional on those inputs and the adopted rule.

A **formal coefficient record** is a sequence $(c_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of
specified coefficients, sometimes displayed as the symbol
$\sum_{n\ge0}c_n\lambda^n$. Unless convergence and an evaluation map are
separately proved and adopted, the symbol records coefficients only: it is not
an evaluated function, exact probability, convergent perturbation series, or
error bound. A formal coefficient can be assigned a phenomenological meaning
only by a separate, model-specific physical adoption with its approximation
scope stated.

An **empirical estimate** is a source-reported number obtained by analyzing a
finite record of measurement outcomes under the stated preparation, apparatus,
calibration, sampling, and analysis conditions. Its reported uncertainty and
conditions travel with the estimate. It is not the exact model value, and it
does not prove the framework used to interpret it. The 2022 Fan et al. report
is an example of a source-reported electron magnetic-moment determination;
this definition supplies no numerical result, uncertainty reconstruction, or
new experimental claim.

Primitive and derived status is formulation-relative. In a selected regulated
model, the regulator, Hamiltonian data, coupling, initial state, and supplied
measurement are declared inputs; an evolution, amplitude, or probability law
is derived only when the construction and adopted rule establish it. In a
formal calculation, the specified masses, couplings, coefficient rules, and
subtraction prescription are inputs, while its listed coefficients are
derived within that formal calculation. An empirical estimate is a reported
data-analysis result, not a primitive model parameter or a theorem.

The following units are examples of types, not identifications of quantities:
a cross section $\sigma$ is area-valued with SI unit $\mathrm{m^2}$; a rate
$\Gamma$ is inverse-time-valued with unit $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$; an energy width
$\Gamma_E$ has unit joule. Only a separately stated convention may identify
$\Gamma_E=\hbar\Gamma$. The fine-structure parameter $\alpha$, a dimensionless
coupling $g$, and a gyromagnetic factor $g_s$ are dimensionless but have
different physical meanings. The name “width,” a common symbol, or matching
dimensions does not supply an exponential-decay law or an equality between
these parameters.

The exact-matrix, formal-coefficient, and empirical-estimate entries have different defining data: a matrix and constructed state, a coefficient sequence without an evaluation map, and a finite measurement record with source-reported conditions and uncertainty, respectively. Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Gamma=(V,E,s,t,\mathcal P)$ be a finite oriented graph with nonempty finite vertex set $V$, nonempty finite link set $E$, endpoint maps $s,t:E\to V$, and a finite list $\mathcal P$ of oriented simple cycles. Parallel links and self-loops are allowed. An oriented simple cycle $p\in\mathcal P$ is a finite closed path using each link at most once; write $\sigma_{p,e}\in\{-1,0,1\}$ for its signed use of link $e$, so its signed incidence at every vertex is zero. Set $\mathbb T=\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$ with normalized measure $d\theta/(2\pi)$ and use product measure on $\mathbb T^E$.

Fix an integer $s\ge1$ and let $\mathcal K=\bigoplus_{x\in V}\mathbb C^s$ with orthonormal modes $e_{x\alpha}$, $1\le\alpha\le s$. This is finite-dimensional and hence separable. Use the antisymmetric Fock space and second-variable-linear inner product convention of [[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The current draft supplier [[lem-qft-fock-ccr-car]] states that, assuming Countable Choice, $\mathcal F_a(\mathcal K)$ is a Hilbert space and its creation and annihilation operators are bounded and satisfy the CAR; that supplier is still a draft carrier, not an accepted result in this run. The finite-mode basis result [[lem-qft-finite-mode-occupation-basis]] constructs the joint orthonormal occupation basis and proves its number-operator eigenvalues from that exact CAR interface. Write $c_{x\alpha}=c(e_{x\alpha})$, $c^\dagger_{x\alpha}=c^\dagger(e_{x\alpha})$, and $n_x=\sum_{\alpha=1}^s c^\dagger_{x\alpha}c_{x\alpha}$. On an occupation label $\mathbf m=(m_{x\alpha})$, each $m_{x\alpha}\in\{0,1\}$ and $n_x$ acts by $N_x(\mathbf m)=\sum_{\alpha=1}^s m_{x\alpha}$; it is bounded self-adjoint with spectrum contained in $\{0,\ldots,s\}$.

The kinematical Hilbert space is
$$\mathcal H_{\rm kin}=L^2(\mathbb T^E)\widehat\otimes\mathcal F_a(\mathcal K).$$
The coordinate Fourier characters $e_{\mathbf n}(\theta)=\exp(i\sum_{e\in E}n_e\theta_e)$, $\mathbf n\in\mathbb Z^E$, form an orthonormal basis of the first factor by [[thm-fourier-basis-and-parseval-on-the-n-torus]]. On this basis define the electric operator $E_e e_{\mathbf n}=n_e e_{\mathbf n}$, with its maximal diagonal domain; hence $E_e$ is self-adjoint with integer spectrum. Define the bounded unitary multiplication operator $U_e f(\theta)=e^{i\theta_e}f(\theta)$, equivalently $U_e e_{\mathbf n}=e_{\mathbf n+\delta_e}$, so $[E_e,U_f]=\delta_{ef}U_f$ on $D(E_e)$.

Fix background integers $b_x\in\{0,\ldots,s\}$. In the joint basis define the real integer multiplier
$$\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)=\sum_{e:s(e)=x}n_e-\sum_{e:t(e)=x}n_e-\left(\sum_{\alpha=1}^s m_{x\alpha}-b_x\right),$$
and let $G_x$ be its maximal diagonal operator, with domain $D(G_x)=\{\psi:\sum_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}|\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)|^2|\psi_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}|^2<\infty\}$. On the common link-electric domain this is the finite sum $\sum_{s(e)=x}E_e-\sum_{t(e)=x}E_e-(n_x-b_xI)$. These are the Gauss operators; the operator constraint defines $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}:=\bigcap_{x\in V}\ker G_x$. For $\alpha\in\mathbb T^V$ define the diagonal multiplier $U(\alpha)=\exp(i\sum_x\alpha_xG_x)$; the next lemma proves that these operators form a strongly continuous representation and that their normalized Haar average is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$.

For each $x$, choose a Hermitian matrix $M_x\in M_s(\mathbb C)$, and for each link $e$ choose a matrix $T_e\in M_s(\mathbb C)$. Choose real coefficients $\lambda_E>0$ and $\lambda_p\in\mathbb R$ for $p\in\mathcal P$. Write
$$W_p=\prod_{e\in E}U_e^{\sigma_{p,e}},\qquad V_B=-\frac12\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}\lambda_p(W_p+W_p^\dagger),$$
and
$$V_F=\sum_{x\in V}\sum_{\alpha,\beta=1}^s c^\dagger_{x\alpha}(M_x)_{\alpha\beta}c_{x\beta}+\sum_{e\in E}\left(A_e+A_e^\dagger\right),\qquad A_e=\sum_{\alpha,\beta=1}^s c^\dagger_{s(e),\alpha}(T_e)_{\alpha\beta}U_e c_{t(e),\beta}.$$
The operator $H_0=\lambda_E\sum_{e\in E}E_e^2$ is the diagonal multiplier with domain
$$D(H_0)=\left\{\psi:\sum_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}\left(\lambda_E\sum_{e\in E}n_e^2\right)^2|\psi_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}|^2<\infty\right\},$$
where $\mathbf m=(m_{x\alpha})$ ranges over occupation configurations with each $m_{x\alpha}\in\{0,1\}$, and $N_x(\mathbf m)=\sum_{\alpha=1}^s m_{x\alpha}$ is the eigenvalue of $n_x$ on that basis vector. The coefficients $\lambda_E,\lambda_p$ and entries of $M_x,T_e$ are ordinary real or complex scalars here; no physical units are assigned. Set $H=H_0+V_B+V_F$ on $D(H_0)$. This is a mathematical finite-graph regulator definition. It asserts no physical adoption, continuum limit, Lorentz invariance, or identification with a particular continuum QED model.

For sign comparison only, if a smooth path $\gamma_e:[0,1]\to X$ in a smooth manifold $X$, a real $C^1$ connection one-form $a$, and a real $C^1$ function $\lambda$ are supplied, take $U_e^{\rm cont}=\exp(-ig\int_0^1a_{\gamma_e(r)}(\dot\gamma_e(r))\,dr)$ for real $g$. Under $a\mapsto a+d\lambda$, the endpoint factor is $e^{ig(\lambda(s(e))-\lambda(t(e)))}$, matching the finite vertex-phase convention when $\alpha_x=g\lambda(x)$. This comparison supplies no embedding of the finite graph into $X$ and asserts no continuum limit.

Assume the conditional compact-rotor/CAR data of [[def-qft-compact-lattice-gauge-data]]. In the joint Fourier/occupation basis write
$$\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)=\sum_{e:s(e)=x}n_e-\sum_{e:t(e)=x}n_e-\sum_{\alpha=1}^s m_{x\alpha}+b_x\in\mathbb Z.$$
For every vertex $x$, let $G_x$ be multiplication by $\gamma_x$ on its maximal diagonal domain
$$D(G_x)=\left\{\psi:\sum_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}|\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)|^2|\psi_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
Then each $G_x$ is self-adjoint, the $G_x$ strongly commute, and $U(\alpha)=\exp(i\sum_x\alpha_xG_x)$ is a strongly continuous unitary representation of $\mathbb T^V$. Its action obeys
$$U(\alpha)c_{x\beta}U(\alpha)^\dagger=e^{i\alpha_x}c_{x\beta},\qquad U(\alpha)U_eU(\alpha)^\dagger=e^{i(\alpha_{s(e)}-\alpha_{t(e)})}U_e.$$
The normalized Haar average
$$P=\frac1{(2\pi)^{|V|}}\int_{[0,2\pi]^{|V|}}U(\alpha)\,d\alpha$$
is the orthogonal projection onto $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}=\bigcap_x\ker G_x$. This subspace is nonzero for every admissible fixed background $b$: it contains the normalized state with link Fourier labels $n_e=0$ and site occupations $m_{x\alpha}$ chosen so $\sum_\alpha m_{x\alpha}=b_x$.
steps: The finite-support linear combinations of the joint basis vectors are dense in $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$. On each joint basis vector, $G_x$ multiplies by the real number $\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)$. The maximal diagonal operator is self-adjoint: if $\phi\in D(G_x^*)$ and $G_x^*\phi=\eta$, testing the adjoint identity against each basis vector gives $\eta_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}=\gamma_x(\mathbf n,\mathbf m)\phi_{\mathbf n,\mathbf m}$. Since $\eta\in\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$, the defining weighted square sum for $D(G_x)$ is finite, so $D(G_x^*)\subseteq D(G_x)$; conversely Cauchy–Schwarz gives the adjoint identity for every $\phi\in D(G_x)$. [F1, given, algebra]

Every $G_x$ is diagonal in the same basis. Thus the spectral projections of any two $G_x$ are diagonal coordinate projections and commute, which proves strong commutation. On a basis vector, $U(\alpha)$ multiplies by $e^{i\sum_x\alpha_x\gamma_x}$; integer $\gamma_x$ makes it $2\pi$-periodic in each coordinate, and the diagonal phases give $U(\alpha+\beta)=U(\alpha)U(\beta)$ and $U(0)=I$. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

For finite linear combinations of basis vectors, $\alpha\mapsto U(\alpha)\psi$ is a finite sum of continuous characters. Such vectors are dense and all $U(\alpha)$ have norm one, so for arbitrary $\psi$ approximation by a finite combination proves norm continuity of $\alpha\mapsto U(\alpha)\psi$. This is strong continuity. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

From $[E_e,U_f]=\delta_{ef}U_f$ and $[n_y,c_{x\beta}]=-\delta_{xy}c_{x\beta}$ on the finite occupation core, one has $[G_x,U_e]=(\mathbf1_{x=s(e)}-\mathbf1_{x=t(e)})U_e$ and $[G_x,c_{y\beta}]=\delta_{xy}c_{y\beta}$. Exponentiating these exact shifts on the joint basis yields the two displayed gauge-transformation laws. [F1, step 2.1, algebra]

For every $\psi\in\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$, strong continuity from step 3.1 makes $\alpha\mapsto U(\alpha)\psi$ continuous on the compact torus. Its Hilbert-valued Riemann sums converge in norm: uniform continuity makes sums over partitions of mesh tending to zero a Cauchy family, and completeness supplies their limit. The normalized integral therefore exists, and its operator norm is at most one because each summand is an average of unitary images. For a basis vector with charge labels $\gamma=(\gamma_x)$, that integral is the vector itself if $\gamma=0$ and zero otherwise, since $(2\pi)^{-1}\int_0^{2\pi}e^{ik\alpha}\,d\alpha=\mathbf1_{k=0}$ for each integer $k$. By density of finite-support vectors and the norm bound, $P$ is the diagonal multiplier $\mathbf1_{\gamma=0}$ on all of $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$; hence $P=P^*=P^2$ and its range is exactly the joint kernel of the $G_x$. [F1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

For each $x$, choose any $b_x$ of the $s$ fermion modes at that site to occupy. The occupation vector so obtained is normalized and has $n_x=b_x$; tensoring it with the zero-link Fourier basis vector gives every $\gamma_x=0$. Thus it is a nonzero vector in $\operatorname{ran}P=\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$. [F1, step 4.1, construct] ∎

Assume the model data of [[def-qft-compact-lattice-gauge-data]] and the Axiom of Choice. Let $H$ be the self-adjoint Hamiltonian on the exact domain supplied by [[lem-qft-lattice-hamiltonian-selfadjoint]], and let $P$ be the physical projection of [[lem-qft-lattice-gauss-projection]]. For any scalar $\hbar>0$, the family
$$\mathcal U(t)=e^{-itH/\hbar},\qquad t\in\mathbb R,$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$, preserves $D(H)$, and satisfies
$$\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\mathcal U(h)\psi-\psi}{h}=-\frac{i}{\hbar}H\psi\quad(\psi\in D(H)).$$
It commutes with every gauge transformation $U(\alpha)$ and with $P$. Hence $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}=\operatorname{ran}P$ is a reducing subspace and $\mathcal U(t)|_{\mathcal H_{\rm phys}}$ is a strongly continuous unitary group with skew-adjoint infinitesimal generator $-iH|_{D(H)\cap\mathcal H_{\rm phys}}/\hbar$; its self-adjoint Stone operator is $-H|_{D(H)\cap\mathcal H_{\rm phys}}/\hbar$. Equivalently, the restricted physical Hamiltonian $H|_{D(H)\cap\mathcal H_{\rm phys}}$ is self-adjoint. This is an exact fixed-graph result; no continuum dynamics are asserted.
steps: Since $H$ is self-adjoint, $T=-H/\hbar$ is self-adjoint. Stone's theorem [F3] gives $\mathcal U(t)=e^{itT}=e^{-itH/\hbar}$ as a strongly continuous unitary group with the stated derivative at $t=0$ and exact generator domain $D(H)$. [A1, F2, F3, algebra]

For $x\in D(H)$ and fixed $t$, the difference quotient at zero for $\mathcal U(h)\mathcal U(t)x=\mathcal U(t)\mathcal U(h)x$ equals $\mathcal U(t)(\mathcal U(h)x-x)/h$ and converges to $-i\mathcal U(t)Hx/\hbar$. The exact domain characterization in [F3] therefore gives $\mathcal U(t)x\in D(H)$ and $H\mathcal U(t)x=\mathcal U(t)Hx$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

For each $\alpha$, the conjugated family $V_\alpha(t)=U(\alpha)\mathcal U(t)U(\alpha)^\dagger$ is a strongly continuous unitary group. By [F2], its generator is $-iH/\hbar$ on exactly $D(H)$, the same generator as $\mathcal U(t)$. Uniqueness in Stone's theorem gives $V_\alpha(t)=\mathcal U(t)$ for every $t$. [F2, F3, step 1.1]

Averaging the commutation $U(\alpha)\mathcal U(t)=\mathcal U(t)U(\alpha)$ over normalized Haar measure gives $P\mathcal U(t)=\mathcal U(t)P$. Thus $\mathcal U(t)$ and its inverse preserve $\operatorname{ran}P=\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$, and the restricted group is unitary and strongly continuous on that closed Hilbert subspace. [F1, step 2.2, algebra]

For $x\in\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$, the restricted difference quotient is the same norm limit as in $\mathcal H_{\rm kin}$. It exists exactly when $x\in D(H)$ by [F3]; therefore the restricted group generator has domain $D(H)\cap\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$ and is $-iH/\hbar$ there. Stone's theorem on $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$ identifies its self-adjoint Stone operator as $-H|_{D(H)\cap\mathcal H_{\rm phys}}/\hbar$. Since multiplication by the nonzero real scalar $-\hbar$ preserves self-adjointness, the restricted physical Hamiltonian is self-adjoint. [A1, F3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

Assume the compact finite-graph model and the Axiom of Choice. Fix a vertex $x$, pairwise distinct real times $t_1,\ldots,t_n$ with $n\ge1$, bounded operators $O_j$, and a normalized physical vector $\psi$. Assume each $O_j$ maps $D(G_x)$ into itself and has a bounded commutator with $G_x$. Let
$$O_j(t_j)=\mathcal U(t_j)^\dagger O_j\mathcal U(t_j),\qquad G_x(t)=\mathcal U(t)^\dagger G_x\mathcal U(t),$$
where $\mathcal U(t)=e^{-itH/\hbar}$. Define ordinary time ordering by placing the factor with the larger time to the left; $G_x$ is bosonic, so moving it past an insertion introduces no grading sign. Then $G_x(t)=G_x$, and, as a distribution in $t$,
$$\frac{d}{dt}\left\langle\psi,\mathcal T\!\left[G_x(t)\prod_{j=1}^nO_j(t_j)\right]\psi\right\rangle=\sum_{j=1}^n\delta(t-t_j)\left\langle\psi,\mathcal T\!\left([G_x,O_j(t_j)]\prod_{i\ne j}O_i(t_i)\right)\psi\right\rangle.$$
The products and commutators are evaluated on the common domains just specified. This is a finite-regulator contact identity, not a claim about continuum renormalized time-ordered products.
steps: By the Axiom of Choice [A1], the self-adjoint $H$ generates the unitary group in [F2]. Its commutation with every gauge transformation implies commutation with the self-adjoint generators $G_x$ on $D(G_x)$; the domain-preserving statement is established in [F1]. Hence $G_x(t)=G_x$. Each $O_j(t_j)$ is bounded and preserves $D(G_x)$ by [F1], so every time-ordered product in the Statement is defined on $\psi$. [A1, F1, F2, given]

Between two successive insertion times, the ordering of the fixed $O_j(t_j)$ and the single variable-time factor $G_x(t)$ does not change. Since $G_x(t)=G_x$, the ordered operator product and its expectation are constant on each such open interval. [step 1.1, given]

When $t$ increases through $t_j$, the factor $G_x$ moves from the right of $O_j(t_j)$ to its left. The right-limit minus the left-limit of the ordered product is therefore the same ordered product with that factor replaced by $G_xO_j(t_j)-O_j(t_j)G_x=[G_x,O_j(t_j)]$; all other insertion orders remain fixed because the $t_i$ are distinct. The commutator is defined on the required domain and bounded by assumption. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

A piecewise constant locally integrable function has distributional derivative equal to the sum of its jumps times delta distributions: for every compactly supported smooth $\varphi$, integration by parts on the intervals separated by $t_j$ gives $-\int F(t)\varphi'(t)\,dt=\sum_j(F(t_j+)-F(t_j-))\varphi(t_j)$. Substituting the jumps from step 2.2 proves the displayed identity. [step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

Use the fields, Fock spaces, vacua, coordinate conventions, and natural/SI
normalizations adopted in [[post-qft-free-field-model]]. For an open spacetime
region $O\subseteq\mathbb R^4$, a scalar test is a real
$f\in C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb R)$ and a Dirac test is a
$F\in C_c^\infty(O;\mathbb C^4)$. These are compactly supported smooth test
functions on the fixed inertial Minkowski chart.

For scalar tests use the bounded Weyl operators
$$W_\mu(f)=W_{\rm Segal}(\sqrt2 K_\mu f),$$
where $K_\mu$ is the future-shell restriction and
$W_{\rm Segal}$ is the unitary generated by the closed Segal field, with the
normalization and phase convention of
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]]. Define the scalar bounded observable algebra
$\mathfrak A_s(O)$ to be the norm closure of the unital $*$-algebra generated
by these $W_\mu(f)$. The real smeared field is symmetric on
$\mathcal D_{\rm fin}$ and its self-adjoint closure has the exact multiplier
domain supplied by [[lem-qft-free-domain-observables]] and
[[lem-qft-segal-weyl-domain]].

For Dirac tests, $\Psi(F)$ is the bounded smeared CAR field of
[[lem-qft-free-dirac-car-locality]]. Define $\mathfrak A_D(O)$ as the norm
closure of the unital algebra generated by products containing an even number
of these field operators and their adjoints, with all test supports in $O$.
“Even” here means even field parity, or equivalently an even number of odd
CAR field generators in each product. The even algebra is the selected local
Dirac observable algebra; an odd charged field is not included as a commuting
local observable.

The selected vacuum states on bounded operators are the vector states
$\omega_s(A)=\langle\Omega_s,A\Omega_s\rangle$ and
$\omega_D(B)=\langle\Omega_D,B\Omega_D\rangle$. For the scalar Fock space,
define the total number, Hamiltonian, and translation momentum components by
$$N_s=d\Gamma_s(1),\qquad H_s=\hbar c\,d\Gamma_s(\omega_\mu),\qquad P_{s,j}=\hbar\,d\Gamma_s(-k_j).$$
Here $d\Gamma_s$ acts on the $n$-particle sector by summing the displayed
one-particle multiplier over its $n$ arguments. Their maximal domains are
the square-integrability domains of those sector sums; in particular,
$$D(N_s)=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge1}n^2\|\Psi_n\|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
The sign in $P_{s,j}$ matches the field translation phase
$\omega_\mu x^0-\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf x$. For the Dirac Fock space, let $H$
and $P_j$ be the mathematical translation generators of
[[lem-qft-dirac-fermionic-translation-spectrum]]. Their one-particle
multipliers are respectively $(\omega_\mu,\mathbf k)$ for particles and
$(\omega_\mu,-\mathbf k)$ for antiparticles, and the sector multiplier is
their sum. Define the physical Dirac Hamiltonian and momentum by
$H_D=\hbar cH$ and $P_{D,j}=\hbar P_j$, using the positive SI constants from
[[def-qft-framework-units]]. Their exact domains are unchanged by these
nonzero scale factors; their multipliers have units joules and momentum,
respectively.

For any of these self-adjoint operators $A$, a normalized state
$\Psi\in D(A)$ has model mean $\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle$ and variance
$\operatorname{Var}_\Psi(A)=\|(A-\langle\Psi,A\Psi\rangle)\Psi\|^2$.
This requires the second spectral moment but does not require
$\Psi\in D(A^2)$. Products of unbounded operators use their composition
domains.

If a signed charge parameter $q_{\rm SI}\in\mathbb R$ measured in coulombs is supplied, the intended
Dirac charge-number operator is $Q_{\rm SI}=q_{\rm SI}(N_p-N_{\bar p})$.
Here $\Pi_p$ and $\Pi_{\bar p}$ are the orthogonal projections onto
$\mathcal H_+$ and $\overline{\mathcal H_-}$; on the $n$-particle sector,
$N_p$ and $N_{\bar p}$ are the sums of the corresponding projections over
the $n$ tensor factors. Its candidate maximal direct-sum domain is
$$D(Q_{\rm SI})=\left\{\Psi=(\Psi_n):\sum_{n\ge0}\left\|q_{\rm SI}\sum_{r=1}^n(\Pi_p-\Pi_{\bar p})^{(r)}\Psi_n\right\|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
This is a candidate definition only; no self-adjointness or proved-domain
claim is asserted here.

Measurements in this model are assigned only when a state and a normalized
finite bounded Kraus instrument have actually been constructed. For such an
instrument, the adopted outcome probabilities and positive-probability
conditional states are exactly those of
[[post-qft-constructed-model-and-measurement]]. They are model probabilities,
not observed outcomes. The field definitions are test-smeared: neither
$\Phi_\mu(x)$ nor $\Psi(x)$ is a pointwise operator supplied here, and the
smearing results do not define coincident products or a diagonal restriction.

Assume the fixed finite-graph model adopted by
[[post-qft-compact-lattice-gauge-model]]: a finite nonempty oriented graph,
$s\ge1$ finite CAR modes per vertex, fixed backgrounds
$b_x\in\{0,\ldots,s\}$, link electric operators $E_e$, the joint Gauss
operators $G_x$, and $H=H_0+V_B+V_F$ on the exact maximal domain
$D(H_0)$ of [[def-qft-compact-lattice-gauge-data]]. Assume the Axiom of Choice
and a constant $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds. Then the physical sector
$$\mathcal H_{\rm phys}=\bigcap_{x\in V}\ker G_x$$
is nonzero. The restriction $H_{\rm phys}:=H|_{D(H)\cap\mathcal H_{\rm phys}}$
is self-adjoint, and
$$\mathcal U_{\rm phys}(t)=e^{-itH_{\rm phys}/\hbar},\qquad t\in\mathbb R,$$
is a strongly continuous unitary group on $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$ with the
exact derivative domain $D(H)\cap\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$. This is an exact
fixed-regulator result conditional on the stated mathematical suppliers; it
asserts no continuum dynamics or continuum QED construction.
steps: To check the weaker choice hypothesis in [L1], let $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be any sequence of nonempty sets. Apply [A1] to the family $\{X_n:n\in\mathbb N\}$ and obtain a choice function $g$ on that family; then $f(n):=g(X_n)$ belongs to $X_n$ for every $n$. Thus full AC supplies the Countable Choice input required by [F1]–[F3]. [A1, L1, given, construct]

The hypotheses in [F1] identify the adopted Hamiltonian, background range and maximal domain with the exact finite-graph data used by [F2] and [F3]; no continuum or spatial embedding data are needed for those mathematical suppliers. [F1, F2, F3, given]

For every vertex $x$, the allowed range $0\le b_x\le s$ lets us occupy exactly $b_x$ of its $s$ modes, including zero or all modes at the endpoints. Tensor the resulting normalized finite occupation vector with the Fourier basis vector having every link label $n_e=0$. Every link contribution to each Gauss multiplier then vanishes, including the cancelling outgoing and incoming terms of a self-loop; the matter term is $-(b_x-b_x)=0$. Thus $\gamma_x=0$ at each vertex, so [F2] places this nonzero vector in $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$. [F1, F2, construct]

By [F3], $H$ is self-adjoint on exactly $D(H_0)$ and its unitary group preserves the physical projection. Restricting that group to the nonzero closed range $\mathcal H_{\rm phys}$ therefore gives the stated strongly continuous unitary group; [F3] gives its exact derivative domain and self-adjoint restricted Hamiltonian. The units in [F1] make $tH/\hbar$ dimensionless. [A1, F1, F3, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

$\mathcal D=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C^4)$. Use the Dirac matrices
and adjoint of [[def-qft-dirac-projections]] and
$$ \Sigma_i=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i,\sigma_i),\qquad S_i=\frac{\hbar}{2}\Sigma_i. $$
The compactly supported spinor-variation Euler–Lagrange equation of the
adopted action, after conversion to SI units, is
$$ i\hbar\partial_t\psi=H_D\psi $$
for this pure magnetic specialization. On $\mathcal D$ its square is
$$ H_D^2=m^2c^4I_4+c^2(\boldsymbol\pi^2-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B). $$
Writing the formal first-order square-root coefficient as
$mc^2+K/(2m)$, where
$K=\boldsymbol\pi^2-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B$, the spin
term is $-(q/m)\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$. Under the explicitly chosen
magnetic-energy convention
$$ H_{\rm mag}=-\boldsymbol\mu_{\rm mag}\cdot\mathbf B,\qquad \boldsymbol\mu_{\rm mag}=g_s\frac{q}{2m}\mathbf S, $$
coefficient comparison gives $g_s=2$ for this minimal tree coefficient.
The equation is an Euler–Lagrange conclusion, not a claim that every field
is a stationary solution. The square and coefficient are formal on the
stated core; no magnetic self-adjoint closure, full spectrum, radiative
correction, or empirical measurement is asserted.
steps: Let $\chi$ be a compactly supported smooth complex spinor variation and write $\delta\bar\psi=\bar\chi$. Vary the symmetrized spinor action in [F1] while holding $a_a$ fixed. Since $\gamma^a$ is constant and $D_a\bar\chi=\partial_a\bar\chi+iq_na_a\bar\chi$, compact integration by parts gives $\int(D_a\bar\chi)\gamma^a\psi\,d^4x=-\int\bar\chi\gamma^aD_a\psi\,d^4x$: the derivative term changes sign, and the connection term becomes $+iq_na_a$ on the right, matching the conjugate-charge term on the left. Thus $\delta(S_{\rm cl}/\hbar)=2\operatorname{Re}\int\chi^\dagger\beta(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi\,d^4x$. No field product outside the smooth classical action is used. [given, F1, F2, A1, algebra]

Put $R=(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi$. If the first variation vanishes for all compactly supported $\chi$, choose $\chi=\rho\beta R$ for any nonnegative compactly supported smooth real bump $\rho$. Since $\beta^2=I$ and $\beta=\beta^\dagger$, this gives $0=2\int\rho\,R^\dagger R\,d^4x$. If $R$ were nonzero at a point, continuity would make $R^\dagger R>0$ on a neighborhood, and a bump supported there would make the integral positive; hence $R=0$ pointwise. Conversely, if $R=0$, the first variation in 1.1 vanishes. Therefore the compact spinor-variation Euler–Lagrange equation is $(i\gamma^aD_a-\mu)\psi=0$. [given, step 1.1, F2, algebra]

With $A_0=0$, the conversion in [F2] gives $$ D_0=c^{-1}\partial_t,\qquad D_i=\partial_i-iqA_i/\hbar. $$ Use $\gamma^0=\beta$ and $\gamma^i=\beta\alpha_i$ in the Euler–Lagrange equation just obtained, multiply on the left by $\beta$, and use $\mu=mc/\hbar$. After multiplication by $\hbar c$, the result is $$ i\hbar\partial_t\psi= [c\boldsymbol\alpha\cdot(-i\hbar\boldsymbol\nabla-q\mathbf A) +\beta mc^2]\psi=H_D\psi. $$ This is an equality of the stated differential expressions. It establishes the QX12 Hamiltonian convention on $\mathcal D$ and assumes no operator closure. [given, step 2.1, F2, F4, F5, algebra]

The smooth multiplication and derivative maps preserve $\mathcal D$. By [F3], their commutator is $[\pi_i,\pi_j]=iq\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}B_k$ there, and the Pauli-block identity $\alpha_i\alpha_j=\delta_{ij}I+i\epsilon_{ijk}\Sigma_k$ contracts the antisymmetric part to $$ \frac i2\epsilon_{ijk}\Sigma_k[\pi_i,\pi_j] =-q\hbar\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B. $$ The cross terms with $\beta mc^2$ cancel because $\alpha_i\beta+\beta\alpha_i=0$, while $\beta^2=I$. Hence the exact core identity in the Statement follows, with every product acting on $\mathcal D$. [given, step 3.1, F3, F4, algebra]

In a formal symbol $t$, square $mc^2+t aK+O(t^2)$ and equate it to $m^2c^4+t c^2K+O(t^2)$. The coefficient of $t$ gives $2mc^2aK=c^2K$, so $a=1/(2m)$ since $m>0$. The spin part of $K/(2m)$ is $$ -\frac{q\hbar}{2m}\boldsymbol\Sigma\cdot\mathbf B =-\frac qm\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B. $$ Equating this with $-g_s(q/(2m))\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf B$ and using $q=-e\ne0$ and the nonzero Pauli spin matrices gives $g_s=2$. This is a formal coefficient comparison only, not a source-reported empirical estimate under the type distinction [F6]. [given, step 4.1, F3, F6, algebra] ∎

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ [[def-countable-choice]]. Use the SI/natural
normalizations of [[def-qft-framework-units]] and
[[def-qft-example-data]], in particular the spacetime metric
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, the algebraic energy-momentum metric
$h=-\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$, and the dimensionless coupling
$g_{\mathrm{em}}$ with $g_{\mathrm{em}}^2=4\pi\alpha$. For a finite nonempty
index set $i=1,\ldots,m$, take future massive energy-momentum vectors
$p_i=(E_i,\mathbf p_i)$ with components in joules and
$E_i^2-|\mathbf p_i|^2=M_i^2>0$. Put $\mathbf v_i=\mathbf p_i/E_i$, so
$|\mathbf v_i|<1$. Choose signs $s_i\in\{-1,+1\}$ and real dimensionless charges
$Q_i$ satisfying $\sum_i s_iQ_i=0$. These are prescribed current data, not
dynamical charged-particle trajectories.

For $\mathbf n\in S^2$, let $q=(\omega,\omega\mathbf n)$ with photon energy
$\omega>0$ in joules and define
$$p_i\cdot q:=E_i\omega-\mathbf p_i\cdot(\omega\mathbf n),\qquad J^\mu(q):=\sum_{i=1}^m s_iQ_i\frac{p_i^\mu}{p_i\cdot q},\qquad K^\mu(\mathbf n):=\omega J^\mu(\omega,\omega\mathbf n).$$
The dot in this current formula is $h$-contraction; in particular
$p_i\cdot q=\omega E_i(1-\mathbf v_i\cdot\mathbf n)>0$. Choose measurable
real orthonormal spatial polarizations $\epsilon_1(\mathbf n),\epsilon_2(\mathbf n)$
with $\mathbf n\cdot\epsilon_r(\mathbf n)=0$ almost everywhere. Put
$\epsilon_r^\mu=(0,\epsilon_r)$ and
$K\cdot\epsilon_r:=-\mathbf K\cdot\epsilon_r$. Define the finite nonnegative
angular coefficient
$$C:=\frac{g_{\mathrm{em}}^2}{2(2\pi)^3} \int_{S^2}\sum_{r=1}^{2}|K(\mathbf n)\cdot\epsilon_r(\mathbf n)|^2\,d\Omega.$$

For fixed energy cutoffs $0<\lambda<\Lambda<\infty$ in joules, define
$\mathfrak h_E=L^2(\mathbb R^3,d^3\mathbf q/[(2\pi)^3 2\omega];\mathbb C^2)$,
where $\omega=|\mathbf q|$, and
$$h_{\lambda,\Lambda,r}(\mathbf q) =g_{\mathrm{em}}J(q)\cdot\epsilon_r(\mathbf q/|\mathbf q|) \,\mathbf1_{\{\lambda<|\mathbf q|<\Lambda\}}.$$
The current draft mathematical supplier
[[thm-qft-example-soft-current-angular-coherent]] gives this energy-coordinate
amplitude's exact norm and unitary identification with the positive transverse one-particle space
$\mathfrak h_T$ of [[def-qft-photon-transverse-space]] by the unitary map
$$(U_Eh)(\mathbf k)= \sqrt{\frac{(\hbar c)^2}{(2\pi)^3\,2|\mathbf k|}} \sum_{r=1}^{2}h_r(\hbar c\,\mathbf k)\epsilon_r(\mathbf k), \qquad \mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}.$$
Here $\mathbf k$ is a wave vector in $\mathrm m^{-1}$ and
$\hbar c\,\mathbf k$ is the corresponding energy-momentum vector in joules.
Set $N_\gamma:=C\log(\Lambda/\lambda)$ and prepare the normalized coherent
vector in the free photon Fock space
$$\Psi_{\lambda,\Lambda} =e^{-N_\gamma/2}\bigoplus_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{(U_Eh_{\lambda,\Lambda})^{\otimes_s n}}{\sqrt{n!}} \in\mathcal F_s(\mathfrak h_T),$$
where the $n=0$ term is the vacuum sector. Let $P_n$ be the number-sector
projection from [[def-qft-x03-photon-count-pvm]] and define
$p_n$ as the model probability assigned to outcome $n$ by the finite
two-outcome projective partition $\{\{n\},\mathbb R\setminus\{n\}\}$.
Then
$$p_n=e^{-N_\gamma}\frac{N_\gamma^n}{n!},\qquad n\in\mathbb N_0,$$
with $0^0:=1$; these probabilities sum to one, the mean photon count is
$N_\gamma$, and the vacuum probability is $e^{-N_\gamma}$. The expected
photon energy is
$$\langle\Psi_{\lambda,\Lambda},H_\gamma\Psi_{\lambda,\Lambda}\rangle =C(\Lambda-\lambda)\ \mathrm J,$$
for $H_\gamma=\hbar c\,d\Gamma(|\mathbf k|)$ of
[[post-qft-free-photon-model]]. If $C>0$, the family has no Fock-norm or
projective-ray limit as $\lambda\downarrow0$ (projective-ray convergence means
norm convergence after allowing a unit-modulus phase for each cutoff), although
its mean energy tends to the finite value $C\Lambda$.

For the prescribed one-charge rest-to-velocity current with final velocity
$v\hat{\mathbf z}$, $0<v<1$, take
$s_{\rm in}=-1$, $Q_{\rm in}=1$, $p_{\rm in}=(M,\mathbf0)$ and
$s_{\rm out}=+1$, $Q_{\rm out}=1$,
$p_{\rm out}=(M\gamma_v,M\gamma_v v\hat{\mathbf z})$, where $M>0$ is the
rest energy and $\gamma_v=(1-v^2)^{-1/2}$. The same coefficient is
$$C(v)=\frac{\alpha}{\pi} \left(\frac1v\log\frac{1+v}{1-v}-2\right)>0.$$
If $C>0$, the cutoff family has no Fock-norm or projective-ray limit as
$\lambda\downarrow0$; the proof below derives this from adjacent-shell
overlaps and does not use the supplier's separate conditional infrared-limit
clause. Its required norm and coherent-state inputs remain conditional on
the inspected draft supplier until its upstream inputs are current. This
prediction concerns only the constructed positive free coherent state and
its count PVM under the adopted physical assumptions. It does not infer that
a full interacting-QED scattering event emits that state or that a detector
realizes this PVM.
steps: For each $i$ and $\mathbf n\in S^2$, $p_i\cdot q=\omega E_i(1-\mathbf v_i\cdot\mathbf n) \ge\omega E_i(1-|\mathbf v_i|)>0$. Since there are finitely many massive terms, $K^\mu(\mathbf n)=\sum_i s_iQ_i(1,\mathbf v_i)/(1-\mathbf v_i\cdot\mathbf n)$; each denominator is bounded below by $1-|\mathbf v_i|>0$, so $K$ and its transverse components are bounded. For the measurable orthonormal frame $(\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2,\mathbf n)$, $\sum_r|\mathbf K\cdot\epsilon_r|^2 =|\mathbf K-(\mathbf K\cdot\mathbf n)\mathbf n|^2=|K_\perp|^2$. Thus the integrand is nonnegative and measurable, and compactness of $S^2$ gives $0\le C<\infty$. [F2, given, algebra]

For the one-charge rest-to-velocity current, put $\mu=\mathbf n\cdot\hat{\mathbf z}$. Its spatial current is $\mathbf K=v\hat{\mathbf z}/(1-v\mu)$, hence $|K_\perp|^2=v^2(1-\mu^2)/(1-v\mu)^2$. Integrating over azimuth and then setting $x=1-v\mu$ gives $$I(v):=\int_{-1}^{1}\frac{v^2(1-\mu^2)}{(1-v\mu)^2}\,d\mu =\frac1v\int_{1-v}^{1+v} \left(\frac{v^2-1}{x^2}+\frac2x-1\right)dx =\frac1v\left[\frac{1-v^2}{x}+2\log x-x\right]_{1-v}^{1+v} =\frac2v\log\frac{1+v}{1-v}-4.$$ Therefore $$C(v)=\frac{g_{\mathrm{em}}^2}{2(2\pi)^3}(2\pi I(v)) =\frac{\alpha}{\pi} \left(\frac1v\log\frac{1+v}{1-v}-2\right).$$ For $f(v)=\log((1+v)/(1-v))-2v$, $f(0)=0$ and $f'(v)=2v^2/(1-v^2)>0$ on $(0,1)$, so $C(v)>0$. [F2, step 1.1, algebra]

The fixed-current, charge-balance, transverse-polarization, and cutoff hypotheses match [L1]. The current formula simplifies to $J(q)=K(\mathbf n)/\omega$, and step 1.1 identifies the polarization sum with $|K_\perp|^2$, exactly the angular convention of [L1]. This is a conditional use of the inspected draft carrier at its actual interface. [F2, L1, step 1.1, algebra]

The proved norm and unitary-map arguments of [L1] give $\|h_{\lambda,\Lambda}\|^2=N_\gamma$ and the displayed unitary $U_E$ into $\mathfrak h_T$. Its coherent-sector formula supplies the normalized vector $\Psi_{\lambda,\Lambda}$ in the Statement. These uses require only the actual mathematical inputs of the inspected draft carrier; its separate Q8-dependent infrared clause is not used. [A1, F1, F3, F4, L1, step 2.2]

By [F5]–[F6], $P_n$ is an orthogonal projection and $I-P_n$ is its orthogonal complement. The two Kraus operators $P_n$ and $I-P_n$ are bounded and satisfy $P_n^*P_n+(I-P_n)^*(I-P_n)=P_n+(I-P_n)=I$. They therefore form a normalized finite projective instrument. The state from step 3.1 is normalized, so [A3] assigns the model probability $p_n=\|P_n\Psi_{\lambda,\Lambda}\|^2$ to its first outcome. This uses a finite two-outcome partition for each singleton event and assumes no countably infinite Kraus instrument. [A1, A3, F5, F6, step 3.1, algebra]

The expected photon energy is the energy-coordinate expectation from [L1], transferred to the adopted free Hamiltonian $H_\gamma$ by its unitary map and [A2]. The cutoffs are energies in joules, so $C(\Lambda-\lambda)$ has unit joule. [F1, A2, L1, step 3.1]

Let $\lambda_j=\Lambda e^{-j}$ for $j\ge1$, and set $u_j=U_Eh_{\lambda_j,\Lambda}$ and $V_j=W(-i\sqrt2u_j)$. The difference $u_{j+1}-u_j$ is the same current amplitude restricted to the shell $\lambda_{j+1}<\omega<\lambda_j$. Applying [L1]'s cutoff norm formula to that shell gives $\|u_{j+1}-u_j\|^2=C\log(\lambda_j/\lambda_{j+1})=C$. By [L1], $\Psi_{\lambda_j,\Lambda}=V_j\Omega$. Unitarity and the Weyl product law in [F7] give $V_j^*V_{j+1}=e^{i\theta_j}W(-i\sqrt2(u_{j+1}-u_j))$ for some real phase $\theta_j$. Applying the vacuum expectation formula in [F7] yields $$|\langle\Psi_{\lambda_j,\Lambda},\Psi_{\lambda_{j+1},\Lambda}\rangle_2| =e^{-\|u_{j+1}-u_j\|^2/2}=e^{-C/2}<1.$$ [F7, L1, step 1.1, step 3.1, algebra]

The projection $P_n$ retains exactly sector $n$ by [F5]. The sector formula from [L1] gives $P_n\Psi_{\lambda,\Lambda} =e^{-N_\gamma/2}(U_Eh_{\lambda,\Lambda})^{\otimes_s n}/\sqrt{n!}$. The symmetric tensor norm is multiplicative and $U_E$ preserves the one-particle norm, so $p_n=e^{-N_\gamma}N_\gamma^n/n!$. [F4, F5, L1, step 4.1, algebra]

The exponential series gives $\sum_{n\ge0}p_n=e^{-N_\gamma}e^{N_\gamma}=1$ and, by reindexing its nonnegative terms, $\sum_{n\ge0}n p_n=e^{-N_\gamma}N_\gamma e^{N_\gamma}=N_\gamma$. The zero-sector term is $e^{-N_\gamma}$, including $N_\gamma=0$ under $0^0=1$. [step 5.1, algebra]

For unit vectors $x,y$, expansion of $\|x-\zeta y\|^2$ and choice of $\zeta$ to align their inner product give $\inf_{|\zeta|=1}\|x-\zeta y\|^2=2-2|\langle x,y\rangle_2|$. Step 4.3 therefore gives the fixed positive adjacent-ray distance $2(1-e^{-C/2})$ along $\lambda_j$. A projective-ray limit would make these adjacent distances tend to zero, a contradiction. Ordinary Fock-norm convergence is the special case without phase adjustment and is also impossible. The energy from step 4.2 tends to the finite value $C\Lambda$; nonconvergence is not caused by divergent mean energy. [step 4.3, step 4.2, algebra] ∎

public_section:
Assume Countable Choice [[def-countable-choice]], as in the inspected Fock
construction.

Select the real-scalar branch of the QFT-F01 physical adoption
[[post-qft-free-field-model]]: one real spin-zero species with bosonic
statistics and the zero-particle vacuum. For a smooth real classical field
$\phi_{\mathrm n}:\mathbb R^4\to\mathbb R$ of canonical length degree $-1$,
that postulate adopts
$$\frac{S_\phi}{\hbar}=-\frac12\int_{\mathbb R^4} \left(\eta^{ab}\partial_a\phi_{\mathrm n}\partial_b\phi_{\mathrm n} +\mu^2\phi_{\mathrm n}^2\right)\,d^4x.$$
The species, statistics, state, and action are physical model inputs. The
present item fixes the exact flat-spacetime free Fock model to which the
later deductions apply.

Use the oriented and time-oriented Minkowski spacetime, signature
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and length coordinates $x^0=ct$ and
$\mathbf x\in\mathbb R^3$ from [[def-qft-framework-units]]. Write
$\Box=-\partial_0^2+\sum_{j=1}^3\partial_j^2$. Choose an inverse-length
parameter $\mu\ge0$. When $\mu>0$, the corresponding SI rest mass is
$m_{\mathrm{rest,SI}}=\hbar\mu/c>0$; $\mu=0$ denotes the massless branch and
assigns no positive rest mass. For $\mathbf k\in\mathbb R^3$, put
$\omega_\mu(\mathbf k)=\sqrt{|\mathbf k|^2+\mu^2}$, with units
$\mathrm m^{-1}$.

Let $H_\mu^+$, $d\nu_\mu$, $H_\mu=L^2(H_\mu^+,d\nu_\mu;\mathbb C)$, and
$K_\mu:\mathcal S(\mathbb R^4)\to H_\mu$ be the future mass shell, measure,
one-particle Hilbert space, and Fourier restriction of
[[def-qft-scalar-mass-shell]]. In the massless case the null apex is omitted;
it has measure zero. The shell measure is
$d\nu_\mu=d^3\mathbf k/((2\pi)^3\,2\omega_\mu(\mathbf k))$.

Use the symmetric bosonic Fock space $\mathcal F_s(H_\mu)$, vacuum
$\Omega=(1,0,0,\ldots)$, and dense finite-particle domain
$\mathcal D_{\mathrm{fin}}$ from
[[def-qft-fock-and-test-spaces]]. The Fock pairing is linear in its second
variable. Creation $a^\dagger(h)$ is linear in $h$, while annihilation $a(h)$
is conjugate-linear in $h$. For $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R^4)$ define the
complex-linear smeared scalar field on $\mathcal D_{\mathrm{fin}}$ by

$$\Phi_\mu(f)=a(K_\mu\overline f)+a^\dagger(K_\mu f).$$

For real $f$, this is the symmetric scalar field whose self-adjoint closure
and bounded Weyl functions are constructed in
[[lem-qft-smeared-free-scalar]]. A smeared field is a domain-qualified
operator-valued distribution; the item introduces no pointwise operator
$\Phi_\mu(x)$.

Define $d\Gamma_s(\omega_\mu)$ on the $n$-particle sector as multiplication
by $\sum_{r=1}^n\omega_\mu(\mathbf k_r)$, with value zero on the vacuum
sector. The exact maximal domain is

$$D(d\Gamma_s(\omega_\mu))= \left\{\Psi:\sum_{n\ge1}\int_{(H_\mu^+)^n} \left|\sum_{r=1}^n\omega_\mu(\mathbf k_r)\right|^2 |\Psi_n(\mathbf k_1,\ldots,\mathbf k_n)|^2\,d\nu_\mu^n<\infty\right\}.$$

The physical Hamiltonian of this selected model is the vacuum-subtracted
self-adjoint operator
$H_\mu^{\mathrm{phys}}=\hbar c\,d\Gamma_s(\omega_\mu)$ on that domain, as
defined by the multiplier construction of
[[lem-qft-second-quantized-spectrum]]. It has units of joules and
$H_\mu^{\mathrm{phys}}\Omega=0$. No infinite zero-point-energy sum is part of
this definition. The canonical scalar engineering dimension is
$\mathrm m^{-1}$; a spacetime test function of unit $\mathrm m^{-3}$ makes the
smeared field dimensionless, consistently with
[[def-qft-framework-units]].

Assume Countable Choice. Use the finite data and notation of
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]]: $N\ge1$,
$H_N=L^2(\mathbb R^N,dq;\mathbb C)$, $D_0=C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
and $W=V+C_0+1\ge1+c|q|^2$. For $u,v\in D_0$ define
$$a(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int_{\mathbb R^N}(\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv}\,dq+\int_{\mathbb R^N}(W+1)u\overline v\,dq,$$
and $\|u\|_Q:=a(u,u)^{1/2}$. Let $Q$ be the completion of this inner-product
space, constructed as equivalence classes of $\|\cdot\|_Q$-Cauchy sequences.
Then $Q$ is a complex Hilbert space and the map sending a Cauchy class to its
$L^2$ limit is a continuous injective linear map $Q\hookrightarrow H_N$ with
dense image. Each $u\in Q$ has weak derivatives $\partial_j u\in L^2$ and a
weighted function $\sqrt{W+1}\,u\in L^2$, and
$$\|u\|_Q^2=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2.$$
Here $g_j=\partial_j u$ means explicitly that
$\int u\,\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$ for every
$\varphi\in D_0$.
steps: Since $W+1\ge2$ and every $a_j>0$, $a$ is a Hermitian positive-definite sesquilinear form on $D_0$: in particular $a(u,u)=\sum_j a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+\|\sqrt{W+1}\,u\|_2^2\ge2\|u\|_2^2$, and $a(u,u)=0$ forces $u=0$ in $H_N$. Thus its Cauchy-sequence completion with the stated equivalence relation is a well-defined inner-product space. [F1, F2, algebra]

To see that the completion is complete, let $(X_n)$ be a Cauchy sequence of its classes. By [A1], choose $u_n\in D_0$ with $\|[u_n]-X_n\|_Q<2^{-n}$ for each $n$. The triangle inequality makes $(u_n)$ $Q$-Cauchy; its class $X$ is defined by the Cauchy-sequence construction, and $\|X_n-X\|_Q\le2^{-n}+\|[u_n]-X\|_Q\to0$. Hence $Q$ is complete and therefore Hilbert. [A1, step 1.1, algebra]

For a $Q$-Cauchy representative sequence $(u_n)$, the inequalities $\|u_n-u_m\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$, $\sqrt{a_j}\|\partial_j u_n-\partial_j u_m\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$, and $\|\sqrt{W+1}(u_n-u_m)\|_2\le\|u_n-u_m\|_Q$ show that $u_n$, each $\partial_j u_n$, and $\sqrt{W+1}u_n$ converge in $L^2$ by [F2]; write their limits as $u$, $g_j$, and $h$. The first limit defines a continuous map $Q\to H_N$, since $\|u\|_2\le\|[u_n]\|_Q$, and equivalent Cauchy sequences have the same $L^2$ limit. [F1, F2, step 1.1]

For every $\varphi\in D_0$, integration by parts gives $\int u_n\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int (\partial_j u_n)\overline\varphi$. Passing to the limit in both integrals by $L^2$ convergence and Cauchy–Schwarz yields $\int u\overline{\partial_j\varphi}=-\int g_j\overline\varphi$, so $g_j$ is the stated weak derivative. [step 2.2, F2, F3, algebra]

On each compact ball $B_R$, the continuous polynomial $W+1$ is bounded. Therefore $\sqrt{W+1}u_n\to\sqrt{W+1}u$ in $L^2(B_R)$, while the same sequence converges there to $h$; uniqueness of limits gives $h=\sqrt{W+1}u$ almost everywhere on every integer-radius ball and hence almost everywhere on $\mathbb R^N$. Taking limits of the component norms in $a(u_n,u_n)$ now gives the displayed formula for $\|u\|_Q^2$. [step 2.2, F1, F2, algebra]

If $u=0$ in $L^2$, then step 3.1 says $\langle g_j,\varphi\rangle=0$ for every $\varphi\in D_0$; this pairing is continuous by [F3] and $D_0$ is dense by [F4], so it vanishes on all of $H_N$, and taking $\varphi=g_j$ gives $g_j=0$. Step 3.2 then gives $h=0$; the norm formula yields $\|[u_n]\|_Q=0$, so the embedding is injective. Finally its image contains $D_0$, which is dense in $H_N$ by [F4]; thus the continuous injection has dense image and all claims follow. [step 3.1, step 3.2, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

Assume Countable Choice. Let $N\ge1$, $a_1,\ldots,a_N>0$ and $c>0$. Let
$Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ be the completion of $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$
for the form inner product
$$a_{\mathrm{osc}}(u,v):=\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\int (\partial_j u)\overline{\partial_jv} +\int (c|q|^2+2)u\overline v.$$
This is the space $Q$ of
[[lem-qft-coercive-polynomial-form-domain]] for $V(q)=c|q|^2$ and $C_0=0$.
For $\mathbf n=(n_1,\ldots,n_N)\in\mathbb N_0^N$, there is a smooth product
Hermite function $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ such that
$$\langle\psi_{\mathbf n},\psi_{\mathbf m}\rangle_{L^2}=\delta_{\mathbf n\mathbf m},\qquad \overline{\operatorname{span}}\{\psi_{\mathbf n}\}=L^2(\mathbb R^N),$$
and
$$\left(-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2+c|q|^2\right)\psi_{\mathbf n} =\epsilon_{\mathbf n}\psi_{\mathbf n},\qquad \epsilon_{\mathbf n}:=\sum_{j=1}^N(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}.$$
For the ground multi-index $\mathbf0$, the smooth representative is
$$\psi_{\mathbf0}(q)=\prod_{j=1}^N(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}, \qquad b_j:=\sqrt{c/a_j}.$$
Each $\psi_{\mathbf n}$ belongs to $Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$, and every $u\in
Q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ satisfies the exact form expansion
$$\sum_{j=1}^N a_j\|\partial_j u\|_2^2+ c\||q|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{\mathbf n\in\mathbb N_0^N}\epsilon_{\mathbf n} |\langle u,\psi_{\mathbf n}\rangle|^2.$$
All parameters are positive real mathematical parameters; this lemma makes no
physical identification.
steps: In [F2] choose $\hbar=1$, $m_j=(2a_j)^{-1}$ and $\omega_j=2\sqrt{a_jc}$. Then $\hbar^2/(2m_j)=a_j$ and $m_j\omega_j^2/2=c$. The eigenvalue from [F2] in coordinate $j$ is $\omega_j(n_j+1/2)=(2n_j+1)\sqrt{a_jc}$. Summing over the $N$ coordinates gives the displayed differential eigenvalue $\epsilon_{\mathbf n}$. In the same scaling, $b_j=m_j\omega_j=\sqrt{c/a_j}$ and the normalized $n_j=0$ Gaussian becomes $(b_j/\pi)^{1/4}e^{-b_jq_j^2/2}$; taking the product gives the stated ground representative. Assume Countable Choice and the data of
[[lem-qft-polynomial-positive-compact-resolvent]]. Its variational operator $R$
is compact, self-adjoint, positive, and injective on the infinite-dimensional
complex Hilbert space $H_N$. Let $(\mu_n)_{n\ge1}$ be its positive eigenvalues
in nonincreasing order, with multiplicity, and choose corresponding
orthonormal eigenvectors $(\psi_n)_{n\ge1}$. Put
$E_n:=\mu_n^{-1}-1$ and define
$$D(S):=\left\{u=\sum_{n\ge1}c_n\psi_n\in H_N:\sum_{n\ge1}E_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\},\qquad Su:=\sum_{n\ge1}E_nc_n\psi_n.$$
The series for $u$ converges in $H_N$ by the Hilbert-space expansion theorem.
Then $S$ is self-adjoint and satisfies $\langle Su,u\rangle\ge\|u\|_2^2$
for every $u\in D(S)$; also $(S+I)^{-1}=R$ is compact. For every
$u\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^N;\mathbb C)$,
$$Su=-\sum_{j=1}^Na_j\partial_j^2u+Wu.$$
Consequently $h:=S-(C_0+1)I$, on the same domain, is a self-adjoint realization
of the differential expression in
[[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]] and satisfies
$\langle hu,u\rangle\ge-C_0\|u\|_2^2$ for every $u\in D(h)$.
It has compact resolvent, meaning that for some $z\in\mathbb C$ the map
$h-zI:D(h)\to H_N$ is bijective with bounded inverse on $H_N$, and that
inverse is compact; here $z=-(C_0+2)$ and $(h+(C_0+2)I)^{-1}=R$. Put
$\lambda_n:=E_n-C_0-1$, the eigenvalues of $h$; equivalently,
$$D(h)=\left\{u=\sum_nc_n\psi_n:\sum_n\lambda_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For every $u\in Q$,
$$a(u,u)=\sum_{n\ge1}(E_n+1)|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2,\qquad q_h(u):=a(u,u)-(C_0+2)\|u\|_2^2 =\sum_{n\ge1}\lambda_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2.$$
The lowest eigenvalue is attained and has finite multiplicity. This selects a
form realization; it does not assert that the differential expression on
$C_c^\infty$ is essentially self-adjoint or that it has no other self-adjoint
extensions.
steps: By [F1], $R$ is compact and self-adjoint. Applying [F2] and using $\ker R=\{0\}$ shows that the closed span of its nonzero eigenspaces is all of $H_N$. If $R\psi=\mu\psi$ with $\psi\ne0$, then $\mu\|\psi\|^2=\langle R\psi,\psi\rangle\ge0$ by positivity, while injectivity rules out $\mu=0$; hence every nonzero eigenvalue is positive. [F1, F2, algebra]
The domains defined by the squared coefficient sums for $E_n$ and $\lambda_n=E_n-(C_0+1)$ coincide. Indeed

Each eigenspace is finite-dimensional by [F2], and so has an orthonormal basis by [F3]. The set of nonzero eigenvalues is at most countable, and [A1] selects these finite bases; their union is an orthonormal family whose closed span is $H_N$ by step 1.1. The space is infinite-dimensional: the indicators of the pairwise disjoint unit cubes $[r,r+1)\times[0,1)^{N-1}$, $r\in\mathbb N$, are nonzero mutually orthogonal $L^2$ vectors. Thus the family can be indexed by $n\ge1$. The bound $\|R\|\le\tfrac12$ gives $0<\mu_n\le\tfrac12$ and $E_n\ge1$. The compact spectral theorem says only finitely many eigenvalues satisfy $\mu\ge\varepsilon$ for each $\varepsilon>0$; recursively taking a largest remaining eigenvalue (which exists because above half its positive supremum there are only finitely many) orders them nonincreasingly with multiplicity and gives $\mu_n\to0$, hence $E_n\to\infty$. [A1, F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

The family $(\psi_n)$ is complete by step 1.1, so [F4] gives $u=\sum_n\langle u,\psi_n\rangle\psi_n$ in norm for every $u\in H_N$ and Parseval. In particular $D(S)$ is dense because it contains all finite linear combinations of the $\psi_n$. Since each $E_n$ is real, the diagonal formula for $S$ gives $\langle Su,v\rangle=\langle u,Sv\rangle$ for finite sums, and then for all $u,v\in D(S)$ by [F7] and convergence of the coefficient series; thus $S$ is symmetric. For $u\in D(S)$ with coefficients $c_n$, Cauchy--Schwarz [F7] makes $\sum_nE_n|c_n|^2$ absolutely convergent, and step 2.1 gives $E_n\ge1$, so $\langle Su,u\rangle=\sum_nE_n|c_n|^2\ge\sum_n|c_n|^2=\|u\|_2^2$. [F4, F7, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

To compute the adjoint domain, let $v=\sum_nd_n\psi_n\in D(S^*)$ and write $S^*v=z=\sum_nz_n\psi_n$. Testing the adjoint identity on each $\psi_n$ gives $z_n=E_nd_n$. Because $z\in H_N$, Parseval gives $\sum_nE_n^2|d_n|^2<\infty$, so $v\in D(S)$. Conversely, if this sum is finite, then $z:=\sum_nE_nd_n\psi_n\in H_N$ and the coefficient identity $\langle Su,v\rangle=\langle u,z\rangle$ holds first for finite sums and then for every $u\in D(S)$ by [F7]; hence $v\in D(S^*)$ and $S^*v=Sv$. Therefore $D(S^*)=D(S)$ and $S^*=S$ as operators; by the unbounded self-adjointness definition in [F5], $S$ is self-adjoint. [F4, F5, F7, step 3.1, algebra]

On each $\psi_n$, $(S+I)^{-1}\psi_n=(E_n+1)^{-1}\psi_n=\mu_n\psi_n=R\psi_n$. Both sides are bounded operators on $H_N$ and agree on the span of the complete family, so they agree on all of $H_N$. Thus $(S+I)^{-1}=R$, which is compact by [F1]. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 3.1]

Let $u\in C_c^\infty$ and set $f:=(-\sum_ja_j\partial_j^2+W+1)u\in H_N$. Integration by parts gives $a(u,v)=\langle f,v\rangle$ for $v\in C_c^\infty$; both sides are continuous in $v$ for the $Q$ norm by [F7], and $C_c^\infty$ is dense in $Q$, so the identity holds for all $v\in Q$. It is the defining variational identity for $Rf$, and uniqueness in [F1] gives $Rf=u$. Hence $u\in\operatorname{ran}R=D(S)$ and $(S+I)u=f$, so $Su=-\sum_ja_j\partial_j^2u+Wu$. [F1, F7, step 4.2, algebra]

Parseval in $H_N$ gives $\|v\|_2^2=\sum_n|\langle v,\psi_n\rangle|^2$. Subtracting $(C_0+2)$ times this identity from step 5.1 yields the claimed formula for $q_h(v)$, because $E_n+1-(C_0+2)=E_n-C_0-1=\lambda_n$. [step 5.1, F4, algebra]

If $u\in D(h)=D(S)$ and $c_n=\langle u,\psi_n\rangle$, then $\sum_nE_n^2|c_n|^2<\infty$ by the definition of $D(S)$. Since $E_n\ge1$, $E_n+1\le2E_n^2$, so $\sum_n(E_n+1)|c_n|^2<\infty$. Step 5.1 therefore gives $u\in Q$. Thus every eigenvector, and indeed every operator-domain vector, belongs to the form domain. [F2, step 5.1, algebra]

Subtracting the real scalar $(C_0+1)I$ preserves self-adjointness on the same domain, and $E_n\ge1$ gives eigenvalues $\lambda_n=E_n-C_0-1\ge-C_0$. For $u\in D(h)$, the diagonal expansion and Cauchy--Schwarz [F7] make $\langle hu,u\rangle=\sum_n\lambda_n|\langle u,\psi_n\rangle|^2$ absolutely convergent; Parseval then gives $\langle hu,u\rangle\ge-C_0\|u\|_2^2$. The lowest eigenvalue corresponds to the largest eigenvalue $\mu_1$ of $R$; its eigenspace is nonzero and finite-dimensional by [F2]. Since $W=V+C_0+1$, step 5.2 shows that $h=S-(C_0+1)I$ extends the specified polynomial differential expression. Finally $h+(C_0+2)I=S+I$, whose inverse is the compact operator $R$ by step 4.2. These statements establish the declared realization and all listed scope limits. [F1, F2, F7, step 2.1, step 4.2, step 5.2] ∎

In [[def-qft-regulated-polynomial-hamiltonian]], the regulator is one fixed
finite mode count $N$ and one fixed polynomial on $\mathbb R^N$. The self-adjoint
and compact-resolvent conclusions of
[[thm-qft-self-adjoint-regulated-interaction]] concern that fixed Hilbert space
and form realization. They assert no continuum or infinite-volume limit. Here
“continuum limit” means a limit of a specified family of finite-regulator
objects as a cutoff parameter changes, together with an identified comparison
space and convergence notion. No such family or convergence structure is part
of the two cited items. This scope note does not assert that a continuum limit
does not exist.
steps: The hypotheses in [F1] specify a single integer $N$, a single coordinate space $\mathbb R^N$, and a single potential $V$; they contain no indexed family with varying cutoff. [A1, F1, algebra]

A convergence assertion for varying cutoffs requires at least a family of objects, a common comparison space or maps between the spaces, and a convergence relation. Neither those data nor a limiting object occur in [F1] or [F2]. Therefore the theorems establish only the stated fixed-$N$ operator properties. The absence of those hypotheses is not a proof of nonexistence of a limit in a separately specified model. [A1, F1, F2, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

Assume the Axiom of Choice, let $Q\sim N_N(0,C)$ be the centered finite-dimensional Gaussian vector of [[lem-qft-finite-gaussian-wick-moments]], and write $C_{jj}=\mathbb E[Q_j^2]\ge0$ for the variance of its $j$th coordinate. For each coordinate $j$ and integer $n\ge0$, its **finite covariance Wick normal power** is the polynomial $:Q_j^n:_C$ defined by the formal generating identity

$$\exp\!\left(tQ_j-\frac12t^2C_{jj}\right)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}:Q_j^n:_C\,\frac{t^n}{n!}.$$

Equivalently,

$$:Q_j^n:_C=n!\sum_{s=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\frac{(-C_{jj}/2)^sQ_j^{n-2s}}{s!(n-2s)!},\qquad :Q_j^4:_C=Q_j^4-6C_{jj}Q_j^2+3C_{jj}^2.$$

This is a finite-dimensional polynomial definition; it does not define a product of unsmeared continuum fields.
steps: Multiply the formal series for $e^{tQ_j}$ and $e^{-C_{jj}t^2/2}$. The coefficient of $t^n$ is the finite sum over $0\le s\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ of $Q_j^{n-2s}(-C_{jj}/2)^s/((n-2s)!s!)$. By the defining identity, multiplying this coefficient by $n!$ gives the displayed formula for $:Q_j^n:_C$. This is formal coefficient algebra and requires no convergence assertion. [A1, F1, given, algebra]
For $n=4$, the terms $s=0,1,2$ are respectively $Q_j^4$, $-6C_{jj}Q_j^2$, and $3C_{jj}^2$, which gives the stated quartic Wick polynomial. The formula also covers $C_{jj}=0$. [step 1.1, algebra] ∎

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the hypotheses and notation of [[def-qft-finite-euclidean-interacting-measure]]. Let $P\in\mathbb R[q_1,\ldots,q_N]$, $Z(\lambda)=\mathbb E_{\gamma_C}[e^{-\lambda U}]$, $N_P(\lambda)=\mathbb E_{\gamma_C}[P e^{-\lambda U}]$, and $\langle P\rangle_\lambda=N_P(\lambda)/Z(\lambda)$. For every $M\ge0$,

$$Z(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^M z_j\lambda^j+R_{M,1}(\lambda),\qquad z_j=\frac{(-1)^j}{j!}\mathbb E_{\gamma_C}[U^j],\qquad |R_{M,1}(\lambda)|\le\frac{\lambda^{M+1}}{(M+1)!}\mathbb E_{\gamma_C}[U^{M+1}]$$

for $\lambda\ge0$. Likewise,

$$N_P(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^M a_j(P)\lambda^j+R_{M,P}(\lambda),\qquad a_j(P)=\frac{(-1)^j}{j!}\mathbb E_{\gamma_C}[PU^j],\qquad |R_{M,P}(\lambda)|\le\frac{\lambda^{M+1}}{(M+1)!}\mathbb E_{\gamma_C}[|P|U^{M+1}].$$

Define $b_0(P)=a_0(P)$ and, for $m\ge1$, $b_m(P)=a_m(P)-\sum_{j=1}^m z_jb_{m-j}(P)$. Then

$$\langle P\rangle_\lambda=\sum_{j=0}^M b_j(P)\lambda^j+O(\lambda^{M+1})\quad\text{as }\lambda\downarrow0.$$

Every coefficient is computed from finitely many Gaussian polynomial moments and hence from finitely many covariance pairings by [[lem-qft-finite-gaussian-wick-moments]]. These estimates hold separately for each finite $M$; they do not assert convergence of the infinite formal series or any continuum limit.

The remaining polynomial terms have degree at least $M+1$, so their absolute value is bounded by a finite constant times $\lambda^{M+1}$ on $0\le\lambda\le1$. [given, algebra]

On $0\le\lambda\le1$, the polynomial $B_M(\lambda)=\sum_{j=0}^M b_j(P)\lambda^j$ is bounded. Using the remainder bounds in step 2.1 and the polynomial identity in step 1.2 therefore gives $|N_P(\lambda)-B_M(\lambda)Z(\lambda)|\le K_M\lambda^{M+1}$ for some finite $K_M$.
